hints: `u.settings` doesn't exist. What does `?.` give then, and is there a `??` after it?
exercises.solution: `u.profile?.email` short-circuits to `undefined` because `u.profile` is `null`, and `?? "none"` replaces it with `"none"`. `u.settings` is `undefined`, so `u.settings?.theme` is `undefined` too, with no default. Output: `none undefined`. Without the `?.`, both reads would throw a `TypeError`.

exercises.solution: The spread makes a new top-level object, so `q.name = "x"` only affects `q`. But the value of `tags` is a reference to one array, shared by both objects, so pushing `"b"` through `q` is visible through `p`. Output: `2 undefined`. Use `structuredClone(p)` for an independent deep copy.

hints: Where is `greet` found, and what is `this` when it is called as `child.greet()`?
exercises.solution: `greet` is not on `child`, so lookup finds it on `base`. It is called as `child.greet()`, so `this` is `child`, whose own `name` is `"child"` (shadowing `base.name`). `child` has exactly one own property, `name`. Output: `hi from child 1`.

feedback.message: Not yet. `describe` is defined in `Shape`, but `this.area()` is looked up on the actual object, a `Square`.

hints: `describe` calls `this.area()`. For a `Square` instance, which `area` does the prototype chain find first?
exercises.solution: For the `Square`, `describe` is inherited from `Shape`, but `this` is the square, and looking up `this.area` finds `Square.prototype.area` first, giving `3 ** 2 = 9`. For the plain `Shape`, `area` returns 0. Output: `area 9 area 0`. This is dynamic dispatch, and it falls straight out of the prototype chain.

hints: JSON has no `undefined` and no functions.
An object property whose value can't be represented is left out. An array element can't simply be left out without shifting the others, so what does it become?
exercises.solution:
`JSON.stringify` omits object properties whose values are `undefined` or functions, so `b` and `c` vanish. Inside an array, positions must be kept, so `undefined` becomes `null`. With no indentation argument, there are no spaces:

```text
{"a":1,"d":[null,2]}
```

options.label: It fails with a `SyntaxError` before running any of it
options.feedback: Yes. `#code` is only valid inside the class body that declares it; using it anywhere else is rejected when the module is parsed.

options.label: It prints `1234`
options.feedback: Not yet. That would defeat the purpose of private fields. JavaScript enforces them in the language itself.

options.label: It prints `undefined`
options.feedback: Not yet. That is what `s.code` (without `#`) would print: a different, missing property. `s.#code` outside the class is not allowed at all.

options.label: It throws a `TypeError` when the last line runs
options.feedback: Close in spirit, but the error comes earlier: the module never starts, because the syntax is checked before execution.

hints: Is `#code` a normal property name that could be looked up at run time?
exercises.solution: Private names are part of the syntax, scoped to the class body like variables. Referring to `#code` outside `Safe` is an early error, so Node reports `SyntaxError: Private field '#code' must be declared in an enclosing class` and runs nothing. Inside the class, a method could read `this.#code`; outside, there is no way in, which is the guarantee private fields give.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is the best candidate for a **class**, rather than a plain object literal or a module of functions?

options.label: A shopping basket whose items may only change through methods that enforce stock limits and recompute discounts
options.feedback: Yes. Many instances, shared behaviour, and state that must be protected by rules are exactly what classes (with private fields) are for.

options.label: The JSON settings file read once when a program starts
options.feedback: Not yet. That is plain data. A plain object is simpler, and it is what `JSON.parse` gives you anyway.

options.label: A handful of stateless helpers like `formatDate` and `slugify`
options.feedback: Not yet. With no state to protect, a module exporting plain functions is simpler than a class of static methods.

options.label: One API response that is displayed and then thrown away
options.feedback: Not yet. Short-lived data with no behaviour is best kept as a plain object.

hints: Ask which option has state that must stay consistent, and behaviour that goes with that state.
exercises.solution: Classes earn their keep when there are many objects of the same kind, each with state that must stay consistent and methods that maintain it, like the basket. Plain data (settings, API responses) belongs in object literals, and stateless helpers belong in a module of functions. JavaScript lets you mix all three freely, and professional code usually does.
